To play, rest the drum on your lap, hang it from the shoulder or waist when standing, or press it down with one knee while sitting on the floor. Strike the smaller head with your dominant hand for the high sound and the larger head with the other for the low; the bass head carries a compound paste that lets it slide in pitch. Some Punjabi styles use an iron thumb ring for the rim sound, while Rajasthani styles mostly use the fingers. On large drums a thin rattan or bamboo stick strikes the treble head and a thicker angled stick the bass head.

卓拉克鼓具有溫暖而富有穿透力的音色特徵。較小鼓面發出的高音清脆明亮，具有穿透性強: The dholak has a warm timbre that still carries. The smaller head gives a clear, bright high sound that stands out clearly in a band; the larger head gives a deep, solid bass, warm and full. Together the two heads cover a wide range, from sharp highs to deep lows. The dholak resonates in its own way: the skins vibrate and interact with the air inside the shell, producing a springy, rhythmic sound. Next to a Western drum kit its timbre is more local in character and softer; next to African drums it is warmer and more finely shaded. These qualities make it an indispensable rhythm instrument in South Asian music, able to drive the music on and carry the swing of dance.
卓拉克鼓廣泛用於卡瓦里、基爾坦、巴詹、龐格拉、查特尼、拜塔克加納、印地語電影音樂: The dholak is widely used in qawwali, kirtan, bhajan, bhangra, chutney, baithak gana, Hindi film music and lokgeet, and also in Hindustani, Carnatic and Trinidadian local classical / Guyanese taan styles. It once accompanied classical dance, and children sing and dance to it at pre-wedding celebrations; in a qawwali ensemble it serves as the percussion. In Indian diaspora communities in Fiji, Jamaica, Suriname, Guyana, South Africa, Mauritius and Trinidad it is commonly used for local Indian folk music, taan singing and chutney-soca.

The bass head is often coated with a tuning paste of tar, clay and sand, or with a layer of mustard-oil pressing residue plus sand, oil and tar, to lower the pitch and produce the slide. Tuning parts may be bolts, or rope and steel rings; in the Caribbean hook screws are fitted to the side of the shell so that bass and treble can be tuned at once. In the dholki variant the treble skin is stitched to an iron ring and the bass skin usually sits on a bamboo ring.

It was once used for classical dance and later became widespread in qawwali, kirtan, bhajan, bhangra, chutney, Indian film music and folk song. With indentured Indian migration it reached Trinidad, Guyana, Suriname, Jamaica, South Africa, Mauritius, Fiji and other Caribbean and overseas communities; in Sri Lanka it was borrowed from India and has become more popular only in recent years. Tuning also differs from place to place: on the Indian subcontinent usually only the treble head is tuned, while in the Caribbean both heads can be tuned.

The dholak is a two-headed hand drum from South Asia, a membranophone, H-S number 211.2. The shell is made of wood and the two heads differ in size: the smaller is goatskin and gives the high sound; the larger is buffalo hide, coated with a compound of tar, clay and sand to lower the pitch. The player strikes the small head with the dominant hand and the large one with the other, resting the drum on the lap, hanging it while standing, or pressing it with a knee while sitting on the floor. Folk musicians and singers commonly use it in qawwali, kirtan, bhajan, bhangra, chutney, Hindi film music and in the folk music of Caribbean immigrant communities.
